The trees generally form a dense canopy, and few shrubs are found, except along more open stream banks. The understory herbaceous vegetation is very diverse and dense with coverage near 100 percent. The 8 to 10 tree species that generally dominate include red maple, sweet birch, beech (Fagus grandifolia), tulip poplar, basswood (Tilia heterophylla), hemlock, and at lower elevations, sweet gum. Butternut (Juglans cinerea), Fraser magnolia (Magnolia fraseri), white ash (Fraxinus americana), and silverbell (Halesia carolina) are also often present but not dominant. Other associated trees of less prevalence are pawpaw (Asimina triloba), musclewood (Carpinus caroliniana), bitternut hickory (Carya cordiformis), red oak (Quercus rubra), and white oak (Q. alba). Major understory trees are dogwood (Cornus florida) and holly (Ilex opaca). Because of the dense canopy, understory shrubs usually are not common except along streams where heavy growth of rhododendron and doghobble are found. Common shrubs on slope areas away from streams are strawberry bush (Euonymus americanus), spicebush (Lindera benzoin), buffalo nut (Pyrularia pubera), sweet shrub (Calycanthus floridus var. laevigatus), greenbriar (Smilax spp.), and Virginia creeper (Parthenocissus quinquefolia). The herbaceous vegetation is the most diverse and dense of any of the five plant communities discussed. Shortia galacifolia, a southern Appalachian endemic, occurs in some coves up to about 1,500 feet or sometimes higher.
The slope segregate of the mixed mesophytic forest community occurs on open creek and river slopes primarily below elevation 2,500 feet, and is the most diverse of all the communities. The diversity of species is high because characteristic species of both the cove segregate and oak forests of the higher, more exposed slopes are found here. Pignut and mockernut hickory (Carya glabra and C. tomentosa), black gum (Nyssa sylvatica), white ash, chestnut oak (Quercus prinus), and black oak (Q. velutina) occur in the slope segregate, but not in the cove segregate (Table 2-3). Sourwood, dogwood, and many shrubs and herbs occur in the understory. Following logging, white pine is an early invader, and eventually a white pine-mixed deciduous forest develops.
